description: Brali Research Watch review batch for 2026-09-16. A fresh 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of strict if-then planning completed full-source review. Brali already has a reviewed implementation-intention protocol, so the finding is used to strengthen that existing protocol rather than create a duplicate. Discovery metadata remains separate from the Evidence Decision.

research_candidates.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effectiveness of if-then plans – in a strict sense – to facilitate fruit and vegetable consumption in adults
research_candidates.container_title: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
research_candidates.review_notes: Full open-access article reviewed through the final PMC/publisher record, not just title, abstract or discovery metadata. The review searched MEDLINE, Embase and PsycInfo, with the last search on 3 April 2025, and included randomized trials only when the intervention used a strict perceivable-cue -> directly actionable-response if-then format and the active control pursued the same dietary behavior change without that planning procedure. Ten articles yielded 12 independent comparisons and N=2,399 adults. The pooled effect on self-reported fruit-and-vegetable intake was small (MD 0.29 portions/day, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.48; SMD 0.20). The prediction interval included a possible null result in a future study. All outcomes were self-reported; samples were predominantly Western European, female, White and young-to-middle-aged; two articles had high risk from missing outcome data; preregistration/report-selection information was often unclear; and the authors explicitly note a possible file-drawer problem despite no strong funnel-plot asymmetry. Included primary reports were published from 2009 to 2019, so the 2026 synthesis is fresh but the underlying trials are not.

evidence_decisions.source_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effectiveness of if-then plans – in a strict sense – to facilitate fruit and vegetable consumption in adults
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Melum SK, Martiny-Huenger T. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2026;23:51.
evidence_decisions.study_design: PRISMA-reported systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. MEDLINE, Embase and PsycInfo were searched with an update through 3 April 2025. Eligibility deliberately required a strict if(situation)-then(response) intervention and an active control encouraged to make the same behavior change without the if-then planning component. Ten articles contributed 12 independent comparisons; RoB 2, sensitivity analysis, prediction intervals and publication-bias analyses were reported.
evidence_decisions.population: 2,399 adults across 12 comparisons, recruited from university and community/workplace populations. Samples were predominantly Western European, approximately 75% female where reported, predominantly White where ethnicity was reported, and young-to-middle-aged. Follow-up ranged from one week to 24 months.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: A strict implementation-intention procedure: identify a perceivable situational cue, identify a directly actionable goal-directed response, and explicitly link them in an if-then plan. Controls were encouraged toward the same fruit-and-vegetable behavior change but were not guided to form strict cue-response if-then plans.
outcomes: Mean difference in portions per day
Standardized mean difference between if-then and active-control conditions
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: The existing Brali if-then protocol can be strengthened by distinguishing strict cue-response planning from generic scheduling and by showing one applied adult use case. Across 12 randomized comparisons, strict if-then planning produced a small average increase in self-reported fruit-and-vegetable intake versus active controls pursuing the same behavior change (MD 0.29 portions/day, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.48; SMD 0.20). This supports the low-cost cue -> actionable response mechanism in that specific everyday domain, not a universal effect size.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: If-then planning guarantees that an intended behavior will occur.
The 0.29-portion result can be translated into a productivity, study, exercise, finance or other-domain effect size.
Any calendar plan or statement containing the words if and then is equivalent to the strict intervention tested in the review.
The meta-analysis proves a unique memory, habit or neural mechanism for the observed behavioral effect.
A fixed number of plans, rehearsal repetitions, reminders, days or minutes is an evidence-based optimum.
The review establishes objective changes in food intake; all included outcomes were self-reported.
The positive pooled estimate means a future well-run study cannot find a null result.
The 2026 publication date means the underlying randomized trials are recent; included reports were published from 2009 to 2019.
limitations: All included fruit-and-vegetable outcomes were self-reported.
The prediction interval allowed a future study to find a null effect, even though the pooled estimate was positive.
Samples were predominantly Western European, female, White and young-to-middle-aged, limiting generalizability.
Two included articles were rated high risk of bias for missing outcome data because intention-to-treat procedures were not used; excluding them did not materially change the pooled conclusion.
Many articles did not make clear whether analyses were preregistered or specified before data were available, producing risk-of-bias concerns around selection of reported results.
Formal funnel-plot asymmetry testing did not show a strong publication-bias signal, but the authors identified no unpublished studies and explicitly discuss a possible file-drawer problem.
The synthesis is new in 2026, but the included primary reports were published between 2009 and 2019.
The review was intentionally narrow: it estimates strict if-then planning for fruit-and-vegetable intake, not all implementation-intention applications.
evidence_decisions.notes: Editorial action: strengthen the existing reviewed if-then protocol rather than add a duplicate nutrition or productivity hack. Make the operational distinction explicit: perceivable cue -> directly actionable response -> explicit if-then link. Add the applied active-control result as a bounded example, emphasize its small size and self-report limitations, and do not export the dietary effect size to unrelated domains.
